title: The learn'd astronomer
hook: tired of the lecture, he walks out and looks up in silence at the stars
tomorrow: how do you grieve someone you never met?

segments.voice: Yesterday, I contain multitudes: a self big enough to hold its opposites. Today Whitman sits in a lecture hall, and something in him has had enough.

A space documentary, all graphs and narration, and somewhere around the fourth chart your eyes glaze. Whitman has that same evening in one short poem. "When I heard the learn'd astronomer, When the proofs, the figures, were ranged in columns before me," with charts and diagrams to add, divide and measure. The lecture room applauds. And the poet, sitting there, grows tired and sick, and slips out.
screen: `ALL GRAPHS AND NARRATION.` → `PROOFS IN COLUMNS.` → `THE ROOM APPLAUDS.` → `HE SLIPS OUT.`

segments.voice: Here's where he goes: "Till rising and gliding out I wander'd off by myself, In the mystical moist night-air, and from time to time, Look'd up in perfect silence at the stars." It's easy to read this as poetry sneering at science. It isn't, quite. In Song of Myself, Whitman cheers: "Hurrah for positive science! long live exact demonstration!" He cheered for exact science. What he walked out of was columns standing in for the sky. The teaching is in the senses he names: the moist air on his skin, the dark, the looking up from time to time, and the silence. For Whitman, wonder isn't a conclusion reached at the end of a proof. It comes through the body, directly, when you stop being told and start seeing. He's alone. He doesn't explain the stars back to himself; he doesn't even describe them. The poem ends on the word stars and lets them be. Knowledge measures the sky; silence lets the sky reach you. Whitman kept both. He just knew which one he'd left the room for.
screen: `HE WANDERS OFF BY HIMSELF.` · `HURRAH FOR POSITIVE SCIENCE.` · `MOIST AIR, DARK, SILENCE.` · `THE POEM ENDS ON STARS.` · then, large: `IN PERFECT SILENCE.`

segments.voice: If you can, step outside or go to a window and look up: night sky, clouds, or a patch of light on the ceiling. For two minutes, no naming, no facts, no photo. Feel the air on your skin and let the looking stay silent.
The learn'd astronomer: Whitman's lecture of charts and proofs, and the poet who slipped out into the night air to look up in perfect silence.
The line to keep: in perfect silence, the way Whitman met the stars once the charts were done. Until tomorrow.

fork.setup: your nephew finishes a school report on the moon and wants to go out and see it. you could read him more facts first. what fits the poem?
options: go out and look up together, quietly; the facts can come after.
finish the facts first; wonder only counts once you understand.
skip the report entirely; Whitman says facts get in the way.
fork.reveal: Whitman kept both: he cheered exact science and still left the room to look up in silence. the looking doesn't cancel the report.

trapdoor: what you thought: poetry versus science.
what it means: wonder comes through the senses, in silence, alongside the facts, not instead of them.
what a scholar hears: the same poet wrote 'Hurrah for positive science!'; the poem walks out on columns standing in for the sky, not on astronomy.

chat.meaning: Whitman loved science, but he left the lecture to look up 'in perfect silence at the stars.' Sometimes seeing needs no names.
